title: CUDA driver provenance and rolling upgrade playbook
author: Aisha Patel
summary: Operational guidance for validating CUDA/NVIDIA driver provenance and performing safe, automated rolling upgrades across Redwood GPU fleets. Covers verification, canary promotion, Terraform/IaC changes, CI/CD gating, telemetry requirements, rollback criteria, and post-upgrade validation.
body:
Purpose and scope:

This playbook documents the end-to-end process for introducing a new CUDA / NVIDIA driver version into Redwood's GPU fleet. It covers: provenance verification, image and kernel compatibility checks, IaC/Terraform steps for node image promotion, CI/CD gating for node image bake and rollout, controlled rolling upgrade choreography, telemetry thresholds and rollback criteria, and ownership/communication expectations. It applies to all cloud and hybrid clusters managed by eng-infra (both preemptible/spot and reserved pools).

Owners and escalation:

- Primary owner: eng-infra - GPU Fleet team
- Secondary owner: eng-platform - Node images and CI team
- On-call escalation: #gpu-oncall -> eng-sre escalation policy
- Slack reaction channel: #gpu-driver-upgrades

Prerequisites (must be satisfied before any rollout):

1. Signed driver binary provenance: vendor-signed package and checksum published to the vendor feed and mirrored to our artifact bucket.
2. Kernel ABI compatibility matrix reviewed and published for every node image variant.
3. CI bake pipeline green for every k8s node pool variant (see CI verification matrix).
4. Canary nodes (2-5% of fleet) reserved and isolated in a non-customer-critical AZ/region.
5. Observability dashboard with the driver upgrade view created and shared with stakeholders.

Verification of provenance (concrete steps):

1. Pull vendor metadata: vendor-repo SHA256 and signature file for the driver package.

   Command examples:
   - curl -fsSLO https://vendor.example/drivers/520.56/signature.sig
   - curl -fsSLO https://vendor.example/drivers/520.56/driver.tar.gz
   - gpg --verify signature.sig driver.tar.gz
   - sha256sum driver.tar.gz | sed -e 's/  /    '

2. Reconstruct artifact in isolated build environment (air-gapped verification job) and compare checksums with our mirrored artifact-bucket.

3. Check certificate chain and vendor code signing policy: ensure the signer is in the approved vendor list and not blacklisted.

Compatibility matrix and test battery:

- Node images: ubuntu-22.04-gpu, cos-99-gpu, rhel9-gpu
- Kubernetes versions: 1.26, 1.27, 1.28
- Container runtimes: containerd 1.7.x, docker 24.x (where applicable)
- Test suites (must pass): CUDA smoke, GPU memory stress (90s), NVML health probe, multi-container MPS behavior, container restart resilience

Example compatibility table (ASCII):

| Driver | Kernel ABI | Node image | k8s | Status |
| 520.56 | 5.15.x | ubuntu-22.04-gpu | 1.27 | tested |
| 520.56 | 5.10.x | cos-99-gpu | 1.26 | partial - see notes |

CI/CD gating and image bake (pipeline steps):

1. Create driver-bake branch in node-image repo and reference new driver artifact.
2. CI: Build golden node image variants (immutable AMI/container image) via bake pipeline.
3. Run integration tests in isolated test fleet (small ephemeral cluster):
   - nvml-check
   - cuda-matrix: sample ops for 1M tokens/second workload mimic
   - kernel-compatibility smoke tests
4. Artifact signing: bake pipeline produces signed node images and registers metadata in the node-image registry.
5. Promotion: artifacts are promoted to candidate channel (not stable) via IaC PR that updates the node_pool module variables.

Terraform / IaC changes (pattern and snippet):

- Pattern: Keep image references in a single variable per node-pool module, use promotion channels (candidate/stable), and require a manual approval step in the pipeline before candidate->stable promotion.

Example variable and module usage (YAML-escaped snippet):

module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal/repo.git//modules/node_pool"
  name   = "gpu-pool-a"
  image_channel = "candidate-2026-02-01"
}

- PR checklist for IaC change:
  - [ ] node_image_id updated only in candidate channel variable
  - [ ] all relevant regions included (or a region-scoped rollout plan attached)
  - [ ] smoke test plan in PR description with owners and rollback plan

Canary rollout choreography (recommended percentages and timing):

1. Canary wave: 3% of nodes (min 5 nodes) in one region, duration 4 hours monitoring.
2. Observation window: 4 hours including load replay that mimics production percentiles (p50/p95/p99).
3. If green, promote to 10% region-wide over 6 hours.
4. After two successful regions, promote to remaining regions in 24–48 hour staggered waves.

Telemetry and SLOs to watch during rollout:

- GPU-related signals (per-node): NVML errors, memory allocation failure rate, GPU temperature spikes > 90C, PCIe link errors.
- Host signals: kernel oops/panic rate, driver module load failures, container runtime crashes, node reboot rate.
- Serving signals (per-tenant/per-model): request latency p99 increase > 20% vs baseline, token loss or truncation rate, top-k failure rate.

Hard rollback triggers (immediate abort of rollout and auto-rollback):

1. NVML_UNRECOVERABLE errors > 0.1% of GPU calls in 10-minute window.
2. Node reboot spike > 5x baseline in 15 minutes.
3. Serving p99 latency regression > 50% or increased error rate > 2x baseline in canary region.

Soft rollback triggers (halt and investigate, do not auto-rollback):

- Moderate increase in kernel tracebacks or non-fatal driver warnings for more than 30 minutes.
- Intermittent container restart rate > 2x baseline but < rollback threshold.

Rollback procedure (ordered steps):

1. Mark the IaC candidate promotion as paused; open incident if thresholds met.
2. Trigger Terraform to revert node image variable to the previous stable image channel for affected pools.
3. Deploy replacement images via standard rolling-replace job with a high-priority eviction-safe window.
4. For kernels/drivers that require node reboots: cordon -> drain -> replace -> uncordon. Use eviction timeouts set to 30m for GPU workloads.

Post-upgrade validation checklist (must be completed within 24 hours after full rollout):

- NVML health probe stable for 24 hours.
- Telemetry: p95/p99 latencies within 5% of baseline.
- Cost/efficiency: no meaningful increase in GPU utilization inefficiency.
- Security: driver provenance attestation artifacts uploaded to artifact-bucket and signed metadata stored in supply-chain registry.

Runbook play examples (commands to run during troubleshooting):

- Check driver module loaded: lsmod | grep nvidia
- NVML health: python3 -c "import pynvml; pynvml.nvmlInit(); print(pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetCount())"
- Journal logs: sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 500 | grep -i nvidia
- Kernel oops: sudo journalctl -k | grep -i "oops"

CI and observability improvements to implement (recommended roadmap):

- Add driver-version tag to all telemetry traces and traces spanning kubelet/container lifecycle.
- Introduce 'driver-canary' lab environment that mirrors production control plane for preflight long-run tests.
- Add automatic provenance attestation step in bake pipeline that rejects unsigned images.

Communication and stakeholder expectations:

- Notify customers via #customer-status cadence for any region-level disruptions.
- Weekly status update during the rollout window to: infra leadership, platform owners, and 2-3 affected product teams.

Appendix: common issues and mitigation notes:

- Symptom: Container-level aborts with CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN after upgrade.
  Mitigation: Check kernel module mismatch (driver vs kernel ABI), downgrade driver to previous stable, and escalate to vendor with kernel logs.

- Symptom: PCIe link flapping after driver update on certain instance types.
  Mitigation: Revert driver, open hardware ticket with cloud provider, and mark instance type as unsupported for driver X in the compatibility matrix.

References and artifacts:

- Link to signed artifact-bucket: gs://redwood-artifacts/drivers/ (internal)
- Node-image bake pipeline: git@internal:redwood/node-image-bake.git (CI job: bake-and-test)
- Telemetry dashboard: Grafana -> GPU Driver Upgrades

This playbook is intentionally conservative: driver upgrades are high-risk for production inference. When in doubt, prefer a slower, measured rollout with longer observation windows.
